from_notes: SOx/NOx + photo-oxidants → sulphuric acid (H2SO4) and nitric acid (HNO3)
x: Sulphuric acid (H2SO4), formed from SO2, is the main acid in acid rain (about two-thirds of the acidity); nitric acid (HNO3) gives about one-third, and HCl and carbonic acid are minor.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.12; NextGen Environment APPSC 14 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-14.txt) p.4-5; app notes 5:99 sub 9 (H2SO4 ~two-thirds)

from_notes: SOx (Sulphur Oxides) ... NOx (Nitrogen Oxides)
x: Acid rain is caused by oxides of nitrogen and sulphur (NOx and SO2); oxides of carbon and phosphorus are not the cause.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 14 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-14.txt) p.4-5; Rocket Environment (src/environment/rocket-environment.txt) p.21, p.63

from_notes: Acid rain SO₂ + NOx
x: Acid rain results from SO2 and NOx dissolving in rain and snow; carbon dioxide and methane are not causes, so only I and II.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 14 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-14.txt) p.4-5; Rocket Environment (src/environment/rocket-environment.txt) p.21, p.63

from_notes: Acid rain gas, not GHG SO₂
x: Sulphur dioxide (with NOx) causes acid rain and is the main single factor; ozone only acts as a photo-oxidant, and ammonia and carbon monoxide are not causes.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 14 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-14.txt) p.4-5; Rocket Environment (src/environment/rocket-environment.txt) p.21, p.63

from_notes: SOx (Sulphur Oxides) ... NOx (Nitrogen Oxides)
x: Acid rain is caused by oxides of sulphur and nitrogen; oxides of carbon are not a cause, so I and II.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 14 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-14.txt) p.4-5; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.12

from_notes: SOx: Produced from fossil fuel burning, thermal power plants
x: Coal-based thermal plants emit SO2 (from sulphur in coal), which causes acid rain, so A is true; R is also true (coal burning gives CO2/CO) but oxides of carbon do not explain acid rain, so (b).
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 14 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-14.txt) p.4-5; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.12

from_notes: [UPSC 2013] Acid rain is caused by the pollution of the environment by
x: Acid rain is caused mainly by sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides (nitrous oxide here stands for NOx), which form sulphuric and nitric acid; CO, CO2 and ozone are not the cause.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.12 (quotes UPSC 2013 with this key); NextGen Environment APPSC 14 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-14.txt) p.4-5

from_notes: Acid rain SO₂ + NOx
x: Acid rain forms when oxides of sulphur and nitrogen react with atmospheric moisture to give sulphuric and nitric acid (pH below 5.6); CO, CO2, ozone and nitrogen are not the cause.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 14 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-14.txt) p.4-5; Rocket Environment (src/environment/rocket-environment.txt) p.21, p.63

from_notes: [UPSC 2013] Acid rain is caused by the pollution of the environment by
x: Acid rain is caused by sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides (option 'nitrous oxide and sulphur dioxide'), which form H2SO4 and HNO3; carbon oxides and ozone are not the cause.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.12; NextGen Environment APPSC 14 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-14.txt) p.4-5

from_notes: SO₂ gets oxidised in air/cloud to form H₂SO₄
x: Oxides of sulphur dissolve in rainwater to form sulphuric acid and turn the rain acidic; oxide of boron is not a pollutant cause, and HCl/nitric acid are acids themselves rather than the pollutant gases asked for.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 14 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-14.txt) p.4-5; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.12

from_notes: Acid rain SO₂ + NOx
x: Acid rain is caused by nitrogen oxides (option 'nitrous oxide') and sulphur dioxide; CO, CO2 and nitrogen are not the cause.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 14 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-14.txt) p.4-5; Rocket Environment (src/environment/rocket-environment.txt) p.21, p.63

from_notes: Acid rain SO₂ + NOx
x: Nitrogen oxides and sulphur dioxide cause acid rain; carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and propane do not.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 14 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-14.txt) p.4-5; Rocket Environment (src/environment/rocket-environment.txt) p.21, p.63

from_notes: Acid rain gas, not GHG SO₂
x: Sulphur dioxide (with NOx) is the gas responsible for acid rain; CO2 only makes normal rain slightly acidic (pH ~5.6), and oxygen and hydrogen are not pollutants.
source: Rocket Environment (src/environment/rocket-environment.txt) p.21, p.63; NextGen Environment APPSC 14 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-14.txt) p.4-5

from_notes: Aspirin Acetylsalicylic acid
x: Alum (potash alum) is potassium aluminium sulphate dodecahydrate, KAl(SO4)2·12H2O, and aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid, so A and B are correct; chalk is calcium carbonate (CaCO3), not hypochlorous acid.
source: Rocket Chemistry (src/science-tech/rocket-chemistry.txt) p.52 (aspirin); PMF General Science 07 (src/science-tech/pmf-general-science-07.txt) p.29 (potash alum, chalk = CaCO3)

from_notes: Damage to historical monuments like the Taj Mahal
x: Acid rain (SO2 from industries such as the Mathura refinery) reacts with the CaCO3 of marble and causes 'marble cancer', the yellowing and loss of lustre of the Taj Mahal; greenhouse effect, global warming and ozone depletion are not the cause.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 14 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-14.txt) p.4-5; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.15-16

from_notes: NO2 may react with water in the rain to form nitric acid
x: Both nitrogen dioxide (forms HNO3) and sulphur dioxide (forms H2SO4) contribute to acid rain.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 14 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-14.txt) p.4-5; Rocket Environment (src/environment/rocket-environment.txt) p.21, p.63

from_notes: The “PFOA” was also listed with some exemptions in Annexe A of the Stockholm Convention
x: COP-9 of the Stockholm Convention (Geneva, 2019) listed perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA, 'C8', used in making Teflon) in Annex A for elimination, with some exemptions, along with dicofol.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.120

from_notes: Scandinavia receives acid rain from UK/central Europe
x: Norway (Scandinavia) is the classic receiver of acid rain, getting transboundary SO2 from the UK and central Europe, which acidified its lakes; it is the books' answer among these options.
source: printed key; app notes 5:99 sub 10 (Scandinavia - Norway, most acid rain among options); PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.15-16
dispute: Most books and keys: Norway (classic transboundary victim). Strictly, by area and deposition East Asia, especially China, has had the heaviest acid rain in recent decades (PMF Environment Part 04 p.15: East Asia remains a major hotspot).

from_notes: Damage to historical monuments like the Taj Mahal
x: Acid rain (SO2 and NOx forming sulphuric and nitric acid) attacks the calcium carbonate of marble, so the Taj Mahal turns pale and loses its lustre (marble cancer); ozone, methane and fog are not the cause.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 14 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-14.txt) p.4-5; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.15-16

from_notes: Eastern North America (US–Canada belt) ... Western/Central Europe
x: Canada (downwind of US industry) and Norway (downwind of UK/central Europe) are the classic acid-rain victims in the books, so I and III.
source: printed key, books' standard answer; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.15-16 (US-Canada belt, Western/Central Europe)
dispute: Most books and keys: Canada and Norway. Strictly, Germany (Black Forest damage) and France also suffered acid rain; the code picks the two classic transboundary receivers.

from_notes: Stones like limestone and marble are rich in calcium carbonate
x: I and II are correct: acid rain corrodes limestone and marble (CaCO3), and burning sulphur-bearing coal releases SO2, a main cause of acid rain. III is wrong: eutrophication is nutrient over-enrichment of water, a pollution problem, not a control measure.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.15-16; NextGen Environment APPSC 14 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-14.txt) p.4-5

from_notes: APPCB state action plan: 123 ULBs incl. 17 municipal corporations
x: The APPCB state-level air action plan covers 123 urban local bodies including 17 municipal corporations, to be extended to rural areas later.
source: app notes 5:99 sub 11 (APPCB plan: 123 ULBs incl. 17 municipal corporations); thehansindia.com 'APPCB to prepare action plan to reduce air pollution in 5 years' (search result); printed key, figures not independently verified

x: 'Eco Air' was the first-of-its-kind youth interaction programme in AP on air pollution, run by Science City of Andhra Pradesh with NCSTC (DST) under the Eco Next mission (Vijayawada, PB Siddhartha College); the other names are not AP programmes.
source: thehansindia.com/andhra-pradesh/vijayawada-eco-air-awareness-programme-begins-590063

from_notes: Glycolysis: Breakdown of glucose to pyruvate.
x: The first stage of glucose oxidation is glycolysis, which splits glucose into two molecules of pyruvic acid (pyruvate) in the cytoplasm; CO2, and ethanol (in fermentation) come later, and ATP is a by-product, not the product of glucose breakdown.
source: PMF General Science 03 (src/science-tech/pmf-general-science-03.txt) p.26; OnlyIAS NCERT Science 10 (src/science-tech/onlyias-ncert-science-tech-10.txt)

x: Human saliva is slightly acidic to near-neutral, pH about 6.2-7.6 with an average of about 6.7 (salivary amylase works best near this); 5.5 is the enamel-dissolving critical pH, and 7.8 and 9.1 are too alkaline.
source: printed key; general knowledge (saliva pH 6.2-7.6, average ~6.7; not in local library)
evidence: local library searched (saliva pH not stated)
